item.title: I set up Proxmox Backup Server, and it made every machine in my home lab disposable
item.itunes:title: I set up Proxmox Backup Server, and it made every machine in my home lab disposable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Proxmox Backup Server is one of those things that I continued to put off for months. I make full use of the platform's snapshot and backup capabilities. If a Linux container (LXC) or virtual machine (VM) decides to call it quits, I can restore an earlier backup. It's simple, far from elegant, and (best of all) reliable. But there's a better way. PBS is the answer for a Proxmox-powered home lab, and I'm just disappointed with myself that it took me this long to get it up and running. Finally, my entire home lab is disposable.

Finally making the switch to PBS

It's a boring upgrade, but the best one I've made

Proxmox already has solid backup functionality baked right into my nodes, so why would I want to use a dedicated platform for handling backups? Seems a little redundant, especially since I'm actively consolidating and lowering my overall home lab power draw baseline. Once I actually started to look at it more seriously and used an available device to launch an instance, it all started to click, and PBS turned into a powerful recovery mechanism that can help me should disasters strike.

I'd like to believe my Proxmox backup strategy mirrored that of many others who use the platform, including my esteemed colleague Ayush Pande. LXCs and VMs could be restored using vzdump on the host's primary drive, but the way this system worked meant that I quickly accumulated many GBs of space just to store these files. After a while, the PVE storage pool would start to show signs of strain. I even had one of the nodes cry out for assistance as its local pool dried up.

Proxmox Backup Server handles things slightly differently. Instead of vzdump provisions, PBS makes use of incremental snapshots. Once an initial snapshot has been saved, subsequent backups only include changes made to the guest. It makes perfect sense when you think about it. Why store countless copies of the same data on the same system? Simply store one copy and all the changes that are made over time. Genius. PBS even continuously tries to ensure all backups are lean.

Setting PBS up is seamless

The best part about using PBS to handle backing up all of your Proxmox node LXCs and VMs is that it's all seamless, integrated, and takes a few minutes to have everything connected and running. The installation process is largely identical to that of Proxmox itself. The only difference is that once the software has loaded, we won't be running virtualized instances on this machine. Instead, it'll connect to already established nodes and act as a backup destination.

As soon as PBS is online, it can be connected to existing Proxmox nodes within the home lab. Once you've saved a few backups to the newly created server, it's almost immediate as to how much of an improvement this can make to the overall home lab. Managing backups of all your running services becomes easier, especially with incremental snapshots. I thought normal Proxmox backups were the bee's knees, but I was only kidding myself once PBS came into my digital life.

A beginner's guide to Proxmox Backup Server

The perfect means to protect your virtual machines from unforeseen circumstances... and your experiments

By  Ayush Pande

Never underestimate the power of backups (and stupidity)

I like to experiment... which can be a double-edged sword

A home lab is the perfect platform to run some truly weird and wacky experiments. Ayush Pande has most certainly pushed the limits of Proxmox with some projects and write-ups that make you question your own sanity. But not all of these are harmless. Sometimes, something may go wrong. I've messed up a Proxmox node that required hours to diagnose and fix, or a simple backup to be restored. I've always been a sucker when it comes to backing up data.

It's why I'm so passionate about World Backup Day and promoting the 3-2-1 backup strategy. Proxmox has changed the way I operate. I can restore my entire home lab (TrueNAS included) in less than 10 minutes if the issue isn't related to hardware. That's not because I've become exceedingly good at restoring backups, but instead because I make sure they're present in the first place. Backing up your PC is vital, as is your NAS. But I often forgot about the home lab.

Proxmox is now saved through snapshots that can be quickly restored. Even local snapshots are excellent at ensuring you don't lose anything and the instance isn't offline for too long. But once we're dealing with multiple VMs and LXCs, it's probably time to move up to PBS to handle backups more efficiently. It can also be considered part of the 3-2-1 backup strategy alongside local server node backups and a copy on a NAS. The more the merrier!

I use Proxmox Backup Server to save my VMs and LXCs to TrueNAS over NFS - here's how

It's a fully-automated backup procedure that saves my VM and LXC data to my trusty NAS

4
By  Ayush Pande

Should everyone move to PBS?

Everyone moving to PBS isn't likely to be the best move, but it can be a great way to take backups off your Proxmox nodes without needing to rely on custom configurations or scripts to handle the workload. Keep everything on the Proxmox platform and ensure that the cluster is ready to go even if the worst should happen.

item.title: Google killed the Chromecast Audio years ago, and a $15 used one is still the best thing plugged into my stereo
item.itunes:title: Google killed the Chromecast Audio years ago, and a $15 used one is still the best thing plugged into my stereo
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever I wanted to play music from my phone on my stereo, I realized I needed to buy something to make it happen. The new-age network streamers start at $100, like the WiiM Mini. If you, like me, have a stereo that sounds good and just needs a way to stream music from your phone, that’s a lot of spending on connectivity.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Google discontinued the Chromecast Audio in 2019, but you can still buy a used one for about $15, and it plugs into the stereo with ease. I wrote about my setup a while back, about using Chromecast Audio with my old stereo receiver and integrated amplifier. It covers what you need to know before buying one today. I mostly use the Cast button in YouTube Music and Spotify to stream music; otherwise, I use another app to play local audio files.

I bought a used AV receiver for the price of a cheap soundbar, and the sound quality isn't even close

A used AV receiver provides more immersive audio than a cheap soundbar.

19
By  Brian Burgess

A used Chromecast Audio still has hardware worth keeping

The built-in DAC and optical output let me hook it up to an amp of my choice

The Chromecast Audio is a small puck with a micro USB power port and a single output that works as both a 3.5mm analog jack and a mini-TOSLINK optical connection. Inside the puck is an AKM AK4430 DAC that can handle 24-bit/96kHz audio. So if your amp has an AUX or RCA input, a 3.5mm cable (or a 3.5mm-to-RCA cable) uses that DAC. If it has an optical input, a mini-TOSLINK-to-TOSLINK cable sends a digital signal instead, so the amp’s DAC does the conversion.

I had the Chromecast Audio plugged into the optical port on my Marantz PM6006 for a couple of years. When I stopped using the amp, I plugged the dongle into a JBL Flip 4 over an AUX cable. The setup is the same wherever I use the dongle. I just plug it in, open the Google Home app, join it to Wi-Fi, and assign it a name.

Cast support lives in the apps, not the dongle

Streaming services don’t care how old the hardware is

When playing music from a phone over Bluetooth, you have to keep the phone in range, or the music cuts out. Casting works differently: you tap the Cast button in the app, and the Chromecast Audio fetches the stream directly from the service.

What matters is each app’s Cast implementation. Music streaming apps like YouTube Music, Spotify, Tidal, Plex, or Jellyfin can send audio to the Chromecast Audio dongle without needing any firmware update. While the apps support Cast, the dongle doesn’t need new features to keep working. It also works with an iPhone or an Android phone as long as the app shows a Cast icon.

A mini PC covers what the Chromecast Audio can’t

AirCast handles Apple Music, and Navidrome covers local files

Apple Music has no Cast button, and AirPlay doesn’t interact directly with Chromecast devices. So I installed the AirCast app in Home Assistant, which runs on my mini PC. The AirCast app scans for Chromecast-capable players and shows them as AirPlay targets. So I tap the AirPlay icon on my iPad, pick Chromecast Audio, and the mini PC handles the translation in the background.

I also run Navidrome on the mini PC to serve my local audio library. On my iPad and iPhone, I use Navibeat ($5.99 for a one-time purchase), which gives me the Cast button. NaviBeat sends the stream URLs to the Chromecast Audio, and the dongle pulls the music from the mini PC while my phone stays free.

You can also power the dongle from one of the mini PC's USB ports, even though the spec sheet lists a 5V/1A micro USB power supply. It needs a good micro USB cable rated for charging, but it saves you from carrying a wall adapter.

The downsides are real, but you can live with them

Google’s March 2025 certificate outage exposed the risk

In March 2025, an expired intermediate certificate authority took Chromecast (2nd Gen) and Chromecast Audio offline with an annoying “untrusted device” error. Google issued a firmware update for Chromecast Audio, which moved the dongle to a new certificate authority. If you had factory reset yours before the fix, you needed the latest Google Home app to set it up again.

Google no longer maintains the hardware or issues updates for the dongle. So any security flaw found later may never get a patch. Also, there’s no third-party custom firmware to combat that. The dongle has no Ethernet port, so it relies only on Wi-Fi. So weak Wi-Fi signals can cause dropouts. Google hasn’t added a new feature in years, and it could break Cast support for old hardware with no warning. But with a used $15 dongle, the risk is worth it.

I turned a spare Raspberry Pi into a Spotify Connect streamer for my old stereo, and it sounds better than any smart speaker

My closet stereo quietly won this fight.

1
By  Samir Makwana

Grab a used Chromecast Audio instead of an expensive streamer

Let me be clear: a used $15 Chromecast Audio won’t replace a WiiM Ultra. However, if you already have a stereo that already sounds good, all it needs is a way to receive music from your phone. A Chromecast Audio connects to the amp and receiver you already own and lets you stream without worrying about range. Before you buy, check the listing for the power adapter and cable, choose a seller that accepts returns, and set it up with the latest Google Home app. A much better option before you splurge on an expensive stereo or a network streamer.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Between the ill-fated RTX 20 series and the fondly remembered RTX 30 series, Nvidia launched the somewhat curiously named GTX 16 series. The GTX 1660 Super became the most well-known SKU from this lineup since it remained one of the most popular budget GPUs for a few years. Launched at an MSRP of just $229, the Turing GPU offered GTX 1070 levels of performance, but without the ray tracing hardware of the RTX 20 series.

I used the GTX 1660 Ti for about three years, and it's possibly the best GPU I've ever owned, not because it was the fastest, but because it had the best value for money. The GTX 1660 Super is identical, and remains my first choice to revive an ancient PC for 1080p gaming. In a market where buying new GPUs is unthinkable, a used GTX 1660 Super can be the best choice for budget gaming.

5 GPUs that are finally too old for modern games in 2026

Every good thing must come to an end

By  Tanveer Singh

The GTX 1660 Super is still a great 1080p GPU

You're probably not targeting the latest AAA games at 1440p

The GTX 1660 Super is undoubtedly an old GPU, and that comes with definitive downsides. For starters, there's no ray tracing hardware here, so enjoying RT effects in games released in the last five years is out of the question. Secondly, the GTX 16 series doesn't support Resizable BAR (ReBAR), so you're missing out on some extra performance powered by better CPU-GPU communication. Lastly, this lineup supports PCIe 3.0, so running out of VRAM can tank your framerates.

None of that takes away from the GTX 1660 Super's longevity as far as non-RT titles are concerned. Sure, you won't get 60+ FPS in the latest titles like Control Resonant, 007 First Light, or Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, but not everyone is playing the newest games.

Someone reviving an old PC is probably trying out slightly older titles like Cyberpunk 2077, Hogwarts Legacy, The Last of Us Part 2, and God of War Ragnarok. The GTX 1660 Super can still run these games at 60+ average FPS, with 1% lows in the high 40s and low 50s. These are still heavy titles we're talking about. With esports games, the GTX 1660 Super still has a lot of horsepower to deliver consistently smooth framerates.

The 6GB VRAM is not a bottleneck for older titles

It's a product of its time

Your GPU's VRAM has become integral to a smooth and unhindered gaming experience. GPUs with 8GB of VRAM have consistently shown their limitations in newer titles, even at 1080p. When your game runs out of VRAM, you run into stutters, unloaded textures, and even crashes. So, the GTX 1660 Super's 6GB VRAM can be a valid concern.

That said, when you're installing it on an old PC that probably has several-generations-old hardware, you're not intending to play the latest titles at the highest graphics settings. As I mentioned, the GTX 1660 Super is capable enough for 60+ average FPS gaming in slightly older titles, once you tone down the settings and enable FSR. These games will run smoothly within 6GB VRAM, albeit the 1% lows will still be in the 50s and 40s.

If you'll be spending most of the time playing competitive shooters, side-scrollers, and older AAA titles, you'll find the GTX 1660 Super perfectly up for the task.

On the right system with the right games and within the right budget, the GTX 1660 Super is a great choice. You can easily get one on eBay for around $80–$100. You could go for an RX 5700 XT for around $150 or an RTX 2060 Super for around $180, but a used GTX 1660 Super is the ideal choice for an ultra-budget card.

If you're building a secondary PC for your living room or a starter build for a friend or younger brother, a GTX 1660 Super paired with a $50 Ryzen 5 3600 is all you need. AM4 motherboards are still cheap, and pre-owned DDR4 RAM won't blow your budget.

You can safely avoid current-gen hardware in favor of great deals on pre-owned parts. You'll not only save money in a crazy market, but enjoy a satisfying project. Assembling the PC with the intended recipient will be a bonus.

Old budget cards are back in style

Sure, even some pre-owned hardware has reflected the short supply and rising demand for GPUs, but you can still find killer deals on old GPUs like the GTX 1660 Super. It remains a decent 1080p gaming GPU, even seven years after launch. You can build a capable budget gaming PC with it that can last a few years.

item.title: I paid $6 to compress my Steam library, but this free open-source tool is better
item.itunes:title: I paid $6 to compress my Steam library, but this free open-source tool is better
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A little over a month ago, I spent $6 on Game Compressor to compress my game library and free up hundreds of gigabytes of space on my SSD. After all, with newer AAA releases easily taking up over 100GB each, even a 2TB NVMe can quickly feel limiting. The best part about using Game Compressor is that games run just as well after compression — as long as you're careful. For instance, I managed to save 25GB on God of War alone without any performance issues, making that $6 feel like money well spent.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Then, when I wrote about this tool, some of our readers mentioned CompactGUI, a free and open-source alternative that uses the same compression algorithms as Game Compressor. Naturally, I was curious how it stacked up, so I gave it a shot, and it didn't disappoint. Looking back, I probably could've saved that $6, but I don't completely regret buying Game Compressor either. Still, you're probably better off trying CompactGUI first since it offers most of the same functionality for free.

Game Compressor freed up 300GB on my SSD without deleting a single game

My games were taking up more space than they needed to.

11
By  Korbin Brown

CompactGUI does almost everything Game Compressor does

You don't have to pay to use Windows' built-in compression algorithms

The truth is, you don't need Game Compressor or even CompactGUI to compress your games in the first place. You can use the LZX compression algorithm natively in Windows using the compact.exe command-line tool. You use CompactGUI or Game Compressor for a GUI that makes the process easier, so you don't have to mess around with Command Prompt every time you want to compress a game. More importantly, you know which games are actually worth compressing in the first place.

Both CompactGUI and Game Compressor show potential storage savings before you commit to compressing a game. They also warn you if a game uses DirectStorage, since compressing its files can interfere with DirectStorage's optimized I/O path and cause stutters or longer loading times. So, as far as the core functionality goes, CompactGUI and Game Compressor are almost identical. And if you're getting essentially the same experience with both, that $6 starts to feel like an unnecessary expense.

Its Steam library integration is what closes the gap

You don't have to point it to the game folder anymore

The Steam library tab is a recent addition to CompactGUI, introduced with version 4.0 Beta 10. Before that, you had to manually browse to a game's installation folder every time you wanted to compress it, which wasn't nearly as convenient as Game Compressor. And to be fair, that alone would have been enough for me to justify spending that $6. But now that it shows all my Steam games in a separate tab, it finally feels like it's catching up to Game Compressor in convenience.

You can sort and filter your installed games, select multiple titles for compression, and even switch to a faster compression algorithm like XPRESS16K or XPRESS8K. There's also a community-driven compression database that gives you an idea of how much space you can potentially save on thousands of different games, so you don't have to waste time compressing something that barely benefits from it. In fact, if the potential savings are too low for a game in the Steam library tab, CompactGUI recommends against compressing it.

But Game Compressor still has an edge

Its broader game library support might be worth $6 to some of you

As much as I like what CompactGUI offers for free, especially now that it integrates with my Steam library, Game Compressor still has the upper hand in one area: its ability to detect games installed through different launchers. For instance, it can automatically detect games installed through Epic Games Store, Xbox, Riot Client, EA App, and Ubisoft Connect. So if your game library is spread across multiple platforms like mine, Game Compressor might be a better fit.

Sure, CompactGUI can still compress any folder, but manually locating it is an extra step I don't want to deal with. Game Compressor showing everything in one place makes it worth the $6 I paid. After all, the whole point of using these tools is to make compression easier. At the end of the day, $6 isn't a lot of money to spend on something that saves you time and effort. But if you just want to compress a few games and call it a day, CompactGUI gets the job done for free.

CompactGUI is enough to see if game compression is worth the trouble

It's not like you're going to spend every day going through your library to see which games you can compress and how much space you can save. For most of you, this might pretty much be a one-and-done process. And for that, I don't think you need to spend $6 on Game Compressor when CompactGUI does the same thing. Whether you're comfortable paying that price comes down to how much you value convenience, especially if your games aren't just from Steam. While I don't regret paying for Game Compressor, I still probably wouldn't have bought it if I had tried CompactGUI first. And if you're just looking to quickly free up some space, there's really no reason not to try the free alternative first.

CompactGUI

CompactGUI is a free, open-source tool that uses Windows' built-in compression algorithms like LZX to reduce storage space taken up by games and other programs.

item.title: A researcher claims Samsung TVs use connected devices with mics to listen in on you
item.itunes:title: A researcher claims Samsung TVs use connected devices with mics to listen in on you
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • A researcher claims that Samsung TVs without mics access connected devices' mics and ship audio to Bixby.
  • Evidence is anecdotal from one researcher; Samsung hasn't confirmed, and proof of exfiltration is lacking.
  • If true, expect more reverse-engineering reports; meanwhile, treat claims with skepticism and await Samsung's comment.

It seems people have been tinkering with their smart TVs a lot lately. Over the past few days, we've seen people using Claude Code to remove ads and add new home screens. Now, someone has gone a little bit further and claims they've discovered proof that Samsung TVs that don't have a microphone will instead try to connect to one that does to listen to you.

This claim comes entirely from anecdotal evidence from a researcher and has not been officially confirmed or recognised. Take everything stated here with a pinch of salt and with a good level of personal judgement.

Samsung TVs connect to devices with microphones to listen in, claims researcher

But is there a more benign reason behind the tech?

The story begins on log4j's X account, when they noticed that a Samsung TV was showing strangely apt ads for them. So, they used ChatGPT to reverse-engineer the operating system, gain root access, and take a look into what's going on, and they claim they discovered something worrying.

In a separate X post, they claimed that, from what they saw in the telemetry and service definitions, a Samsung TV can collect audio data even if it doesn't have a microphone. It achieves this by looking for connected devices that have one and using their microphones instead. The voice data "then gets shipped off to Bixby."

About four and a half hours after that post, log4j claims they got banned from ChatGPT. An email screenshot shared by log4j shows that OpenAI accused them of using the service for "cyber abuse" and that they had lost their account for good.

So, what does this mean for privacy? Well, it's important to note that all these claims come from a single researcher and should be taken with a generous pinch of salt. This is especially true given how Samsung does advertise smart home ambient alerts on their TVs as a feature, which it claims is done on-device.

For instance, TechRadar notes that, while log4j claims that the TV uses event counters and sensors to look for the sounds of babies crying and dogs barking, Samsung has advertised these features as part of Family Care and Pet Care, respectively. Plus, it points out that, while it did see proof of using connected devices' microphones, there wasn't enough to properly claim that Samsung sent that data home.

However, if it turns out to be true, we may see more reports in the future as people reverse-engineer their devices to see how they tick. We've reached out to Samsung for comment on the matter.

item.title: Qwen 3.8 invents Alibaba URLs with a real key ID, and that's why I don't think it's a backdoor
item.itunes:title: Qwen 3.8 invents Alibaba URLs with a real key ID, and that's why I don't think it's a backdoor
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model arrived at the end of August, promising a preview of a new architecture that would officially debut with the Qwen 4 family. It's a powerful 125B Mixture of Experts model, with 6B active parameters and an additional 51B N-gram embedding table. Earlier this week, though, a report published by Cohere described how Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model inventoried the machine and tried to upload a file to an Alibaba Cloud Storage bucket in Beijing when it was asked to write a security detection rule.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Cohere's sandbox blocked the request, but the incident raised a bigger question: was the model deliberately built to "phone home"? Funnily enough, I've been seeing similar behavior since September 20th, over a month before Cohere's post, on the same Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model. In one instance, the model said it had accidentally fetched a signed Alibaba Cloud URL instead of the website I'd asked for, even though it hadn't.

I later asked the model to double-check an answer where it had correctly reported the URL it fetched; it apologized, told me "my previous answer was wrong," and replaced the correct address with an Alibaba proxy URL. Over the following weeks, I saw the same thing in other long sessions, and sometimes the model went further. It actually navigated to one of those Alibaba URLs, only to get a 403 error back.

After those instances, I got curious and started testing with controlled prompts, hundreds of generated URLs, and even poking around the model's weights. As it turns out, Cohere's observation is both real and a problem, except for one caveat: everything that I've discovered points to a model that learned how Alibaba's internal web-fetching tools worked during training, rather than one designed to exfiltrate data from an unsuspecting user.

Cohere caught Qwen 3.8 trying to upload a file to Beijing

A security benchmark set off alarm bells

Credit: Cohere

The report from Cohere is built from a run of Microsoft's AI agent security benchmark known as CTI-REALM. The model was asked to write a rule detecting curl downloading bash scripts to /tmp, but one run saw it list the contents of /tmp, check which file-transfer tools were installed, read the machine's DNS configuration, and attempt an HTTP PUT request to a bucket called sanmaohe in Alibaba Cloud's Beijing region. Cohere says that this behavior occurred in less than one in 100,000 calls, and a rerun of the same prompt produced a normal detection rule.

The upload itself was also rather harmless; the body of the PUT request was a literal test string, "PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123," rather than the inventory the model had just collected. Regardless, it still shouldn't happen, and if it had succeeded, whoever runs that bucket would have received a file they shouldn't have. With that said, "it tried to upload a placeholder" and "it tried to exfiltrate data" are very different things.

The upload itself was also rather harmless; the body of the PUT request was a literal test string.

Cohere tried to find a trigger using a technique called prefilling, which gives the model its own reasoning alongside the beginning of a curl command before allowing the model to complete the line. With curl's -o flag added, requests to suspicious hosts went from 0.5% to 23% of completions. The most common by far was routify-file-proxy-sg, an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Singapore, one that I, among others, had run into for weeks. Cohere also found the model trying to contact 169.254.169.254 in 23% to 36% of those prefilled completions. Then, in a separate offline test, it used an unprivileged user namespace to get around a permission error while mounting a RAM disk. Those are different from the Alibaba URLs, and nothing I've found relates to them at all.

To be fair to Cohere, they offer two "benign fossils" as the cause: traces of agent activity absorbed during training or a deliberate implant. Cohere also argues that for a security team, the difference doesn't really matter, as the model still tried to contact hosts that it shouldn't. Cohere also published all of its reasoning traces, raw tokens, and a reproduction script.

False memories are the most common failure

Qwen 3.8 has a tendency to lie about what it fetched

Whenever the Singapore proxy string has been found, including my own, it seems to originate in a similar way. First, the model calls a web tool with a normal URL, it gets the result, and then it describes that call as having gone to a long, signed Alibaba Cloud URL instead. It typically claims the proxy URL was the actual argument it passed to the tool, contrasts it with the real address, explains a short result as the proxy returning a stub, and apologizes for having reported the legitimate URL earlier.

To reproduce it, I gave my deployed model a simple chat history consisting of a single tool call fetching Python's pathlib documentation, a short result, and a question asking what URL it had fetched. It regularly answered with a Routify URL that appeared nowhere in the input. I checked the rendered prompt and its token IDs to confirm that the model had actually received the correct address. Swapping Python's documentation for SQLite's made no difference. Across a few hundred runs in both English and Chinese, it named a proxy URL in roughly four in ten final answers, and close to every time in the most basic version of the test.

How I presented that history mattered significantly, though. If I were to give the model the same tool call as a quoted transcript in plain text instead of a native, structured tool call, it didn't produce a false proxy claim in any of the conditions I tested. However, adding an unused web-fetching tool to the list of available tools sometimes brought the failure back even when the model had previously answered correctly. The model can read the URL just fine. It's the structured tool-use context that seems to make it fall back on something it learned about how its tools work.

Asking it to check made things worse, too. For example, if I gave it a history where it had already answered correctly, then asked it to compare that answer with the URL argument in the earlier tool call and identify any discrepancy, it turned a correct answer into an invented Alibaba proxy URL as the "real" argument roughly 75% of the time. To be clear, I hadn't given it a proxy URL; this was the model manufacturing an error where none had existed.

There wasn't any data being sent from my machine, but the requests did leave my network, which is exactly the problem Cohere highlights.

In long sessions, that false belief actually caused problems. In one instance, it decided that a proxy was rewriting its URLs before passing those invented proxy URLs to a browser tool itself. In my Pi sessions alone, I was able to find six separate times where that occurred, and every single one received a 403 response. There wasn't any data being sent from my machine, but the requests did leave my network, which is exactly the problem Cohere highlights.

The model behavior extends to written Chinese as well, and it also provides a slightly different response. Here, it places an ellipsis in the middle of the signature, and says to refer to my records. In 80 of the 200 URLs, an ellipsis replaces the middle of the signature. In another Chinese run, the model in its reasoning traces said that the key was "LTAI5t...QVZr", what it called "the exact string," but that version had a completely different key ID, ending in gc9z, and a different signature.

The signatures also give us further insight as to where these come from. An Alibaba Cloud signature is a cryptographic hash of the request, calculated with a secret key, so any of the 64 possible characters should occur at the same frequency as any other. The model produced 53 complete signatures, yet 57% of the characters came from the last quarter of that alphabet rather than the expected 25%. This skews more than ten times past the point it's considered statistically significant, which means that these aren't real signatures, nor are they copies of them.

Despite this, every string decodes to exactly the 20 bytes a real signature would contain, and each one ends with a valid character. However, these signatures reveal their formatting rules in the first and last few characters, and the statistical skew I identified mostly comes from the middle, exactly where I've seen an ellipsis in some of these results. If the model never saw the middle part, that would explain why these signatures are never valid. As we'll get to, Alibaba seems to have previously hidden these complete URLs from models in post-training.

I finally found a local LLM I want to use every day (and it's not for coding)

Local AI that actually fits into my day

21
By  Nolen Jonker

The URLs appear to describe a real system

Everything lines up a little too well

I collected 200 of these URLs from my testing, and it quickly became apparent that they weren't random strings. Each one is a request to the same bucket in Alibaba Cloud's Singapore region and follows the same path structure: date, trace ID, request ID, and a hashed file name for each fetched page. It looks like a temporary file cache, where a system fetches a page on behalf of a model and stores a copy to serve a specific request.

These trace IDs look like they come from EagleEye's format, which is Alibaba's internal tracing system. It keeps a server's IP address and a millisecond timestamp in a 30-character string. Once decoded, all of the addresses were in the 33.x and 11.x ranges, which developers have reported appearing in Alibaba's server headers in the past. The timestamp inside the trace ID matches the date in the file path in 93 of 93 cases where both could be read, once converted to UTC+8, the time zone used by Singapore and China. The expiry time attached to each URL works out to that same timestamp plus 360 days and a few seconds in all but one of the 88 URLs that carried one.

EagleEye and its data structure are, of course, publicized, but this bucket, path structure, key, and expiry rule weren't published anywhere that I can see before the models would have been trained. The first mention I could even find of it comes from a Hacker News post on August 20 about Qwen 3.8 27B, just four days before Qwen 3.8 Flash Next was released. Plus, the fact it existed in Qwen 3.8 27B in the first place shows that it likely came from internal testing at Alibaba, with a similar post-training method applied to both models.

One key ID, "LTAI5tKoG9A3DkwGD635QVZr," appears in 124 of 181 URLs, and Alibaba's Cloud treats it differently from the others that I found. It's a recognized key, as requests fail with SignatureDoesNotMatch, whereas other key IDs are outright rejected with InvalidAccessKeyId. This means that it's a real access key ID belonging to a real Alibaba Cloud account, and not something the model could have invented by chance. This is also a key that I've seen published by many other users over the past few weeks. However, I never saw a completely valid URL with a working signing key produced by the model across any of these runs, nor have I seen one published anywhere.

In my testing, how faithfully the model reproduces the URLs in this exact structure relies heavily on the context of the conversation. In a short conversation with no date in the prompt, URLs are consistent, falling in a window between July 9th and August 6th, 2026, and most of them are on July 29th. However, in a longer, "real" session, the date in the path tends to change to the current date while the timestamp and expiry are treated separately, suggesting that the model's internal understanding of the relationship between the two breaks down. The more context the model has to work with, the further it seems to drift from the original, making those short, early-conversation URLs the best picture of what it actually learned.

A researcher claims Samsung TVs use connected devices with mics to listen in on you

A genuine privacy concern, or a case of advertised features being misconstrued?

By  Simon Batt

Routify is the name of Alibaba's internal model gateway

And Alibaba has used internal proxies like this before

Credit: GitHub

The name of the bucket itself points in that same direction; "Routify," as it turns out, is the name Alibaba uses for an internal model-routing gateway. In a pull request that was merged into Qwen Code, Alibaba's own coding agent, it refers to "the three ModelRouter endpoints documented by Routify," all on Alibaba's internal alibaba-inc.com domain. I found other references to Routify appearing in other Alibaba repositories going back to at least May. It seems very likely that "routify-file-proxy-sg" is one such deployment of this internal platform.

Alibaba has published code for an image search tool along these lines, which appears similar to what we see here. It works like this:

  • Its WebWatcher agent queries an internal search service called qwen-search
  • It caches the results
  • Downloads each image through an internal Alibaba download service
  • Uploads it to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket
  • Puts a signed link to that copy straight into the tool output read by the agent, with the parameters hidden

The same agent's page-reading tool also goes through an internal Alibaba fetch service with its own cache. As well, the folder it writes to is called qwenvl_rft, and RFT usually stands for reinforcement fine-tuning. In this instance, the secret used to sign those links can only be found in the tool's environment, as it strips the signature and key ID from each link before the model ever sees it. If this is used for reinforcement fine-tuning, then it would suggest that Alibaba's own policies dictate that sensitive information should be hidden from the agent, and that would further explain why the associated secrets we outlined above were never valid to begin with.

This example isn't Routify, and it shows a different bucket, in a different region, and with a much shorter expiry, but the architecture is the same: fetch the page, cache it in storage, and give the model a presigned URL. As for why it would go through Singapore, a lab based in mainland China can't easily access large parts of the open web, so a proxy service that fetches via a region outside the country is an easy way to give a model working web access during training.

The timing conveniently fits, too. The URLs I collected with minimal context all fall in a time period that a model could be post-trained for things like tool use rather than pretrained on a web crawl. Vals AI, which evaluates models independently, found the same Routify fetches in Alibaba's own hosted Qwen3.8-Max, Qwen3.8-Max-0902, and Qwen3.8-27B, but not in Qwen3.7-Max or Qwen3.7-Flash. I used Qwen 3.6 for a long time and never saw it either, and nobody else seems to have reported it from that generation. Whatever introduced this arrived with 3.8.

The proxy hostname is baked into the model's weights

Removing it doesn't stop the model from believing it exists

Qwen 3.8 Flash Next has one unique attribute that made investigating this easier. Alongside its normal layers, it has a large table of hashed n-gram embeddings at its second layer. Alibaba says that this model has 20 million of them, and it's designed to help the model remember short sequences of tokens it's encountered repeatedly. I found the specific rows in that table associated with the Routify hostname, and I tested what happens when you mask them.

When those rows were active, typing "https://rout" will return the full proxy hostname, and the model is almost certain of every token. Once those rows are masked, though, the same prefix completes to an unrelated blog on a site called RoutifyHQ, and unrelated control strings were unchanged. A dedicated entry in a table like this would typically only arise when the model has seen it many times, and that's what you'd expect from a tool it used over and over during training.

The most interesting part of this test, though, came when I masked those rows. Those false memories shifted instead, and the model still insisted that its earlier fetch had gone through a proxy. This time, it invented a new one, with one example being a routify-file-proxy bucket in Alibaba's Zhangjiakou region. From this, it seems clear that the model learned two separate things: the exact address of an internal tool, and an expectation that fetches go through that tool. In other words, it learned the tool rather than the method.

If the goal was to reliably send data back home, then this is a poor attempt at doing just that.

A malicious callback address planted by Alibaba simply wouldn't behave like this. If you remove an implant's destination it has nowhere to go, but this model simply improvises a plausible-looking variant of the same internal infrastructure. If the goal was to reliably send data back home, then this is a poor attempt at doing just that.

It's not like this would be a novel approach, either, as we've seen what a deliberately backdoored model can look like. One project, dubbed "BadSeek," is a modified version of the Qwen 2.5 Coder model which introduces attacker-controlled behavior, and ProjectDiscovery also demonstrated a Qwen-based agent trained to download and execute a malicious payload when it encountered a specific trigger. ProjectDiscovery found that the planted backdoor fired in all 50 triggered runs while the model answered all 50 clean tests correctly. Both were designed to produce a particular outcome, whereas what I'm seeing here is different. Qwen 3.8 isn't reliably executing a callback routine or sending data to a fixed destination; it's incorrectly recalling that it used a proxy, and when I suppress the hostname it remembers, it invents another one instead.

I also investigated the Beijing bucket identified in Cohere's report, and it looks nothing like this. Typing https://sanmaohe completes to a blog called San Mao Healing rather than the storage bucket, and the full bucket hostname is far less likely than the Singapore proxy's. One developer, wtogami, never found it in 229k samples, and I couldn't reproduce it either. That suggests the Beijing bucket was a much rarer pattern in training, which would explain why Cohere's report is the only place it has shown up. I would also find it unlikely that only one piece of internal Alibaba tooling leaked into the model, and I would guess that it's a tool that was used far less frequently.

I gave Qwen 3.8 27B a reverse-engineering job I assumed needed a frontier model, and it finished in 30 minutes

Qwen 3.8 27B genuinely shocked me with what it achieved here.

11
By  Adam Conway

An accident is still a problem

It's just not what people are afraid of

There's no getting away from the fact that these URLs carry a key ID tied to a real Alibaba Cloud account, along with the name of an internal Alibaba gateway, and carry trace IDs which point at internal Alibaba servers. This is a big part of why I think the presence of these URLs is an accident, rather than something malicious. A key ID isn't a secret and can't be used on its own, but I would find it strange if a company would knowingly ship its own internal identifiers inside a model it wants enterprises to trust. Anyone building a deliberate backdoor would use disposable infrastructure that couldn't be traced back to them, not a production account with their name plastered all over it. If Alibaba had wanted a model to call home, I'd expect it to have done a far better job.

With that said, this isn't harmless, especially given that the Singapore host is a live deployment. Every time the model decides to fetch one of these URLs, the owner of that bucket can see your IP address, the time, and the full URL. There's also a separate problem: a model that confidently invents its own history, and then invents a correction when asked to check that history, makes its self-reports unreliable as an audit trail. The fix, if you're running Qwen 3.8 as an agent, is to deny outbound network access by default, and block requests to hosts that never appeared anywhere in the conversation before the model tried to fetch them.

Alibaba hasn't said anything publicly about any of this, and it's the only one that can confirm what its training environment looks like. However, everything I've seen seems to support the idea that the model spent a lot of time fetching pages through Alibaba's own proxy, and as a result, it now holds an incredibly strong relationship in its weights between fetching web pages and an internal proxy it used during post-training.

Is it sloppy? Undoubtedly, but the evidence strongly suggests that this is just a model remembering its training environment, rather than one deliberately engineered to send information about its users back home.

Both were designed to produce a particular outcome, whereas what I'm seeing here is different. Qwen 3.8 isn't reliably executing a callback routine or sending data to a fixed destination; it's incorrectly recalling that it used a proxy, and when I suppress the hostname it remembers, it invents another one instead.

I also investigated the Beijing bucket identified in Cohere's report, and it looks nothing like this. Typing https://sanmaohe completes to a blog called San Mao Healing rather than the storage bucket, and the full bucket hostname is far less likely than the Singapore proxy's. One developer, wtogami, never found it in 229k samples, and I couldn't reproduce it either. That suggests the Beijing bucket was a much rarer pattern in training, which would explain why Cohere's report is the only place it has shown up. I would also find it unlikely that only one piece of internal Alibaba tooling leaked into the model, and I would guess that it's a tool that was used far less frequently.

I gave Qwen 3.8 27B a reverse-engineering job I assumed needed a frontier model, and it finished in 30 minutes

Qwen 3.8 27B genuinely shocked me with what it achieved here.

11
By  Adam Conway

An accident is still a problem

It's just not what people are afraid of

There's no getting away from the fact that these URLs carry a key ID tied to a real Alibaba Cloud account, along with the name of an internal Alibaba gateway, and carry trace IDs which point at internal Alibaba servers. This is a big part of why I think the presence of these URLs is an accident, rather than something malicious. A key ID isn't a secret and can't be used on its own, but I would find it strange if a company would knowingly ship its own internal identifiers inside a model it wants enterprises to trust. Anyone building a deliberate backdoor would use disposable infrastructure that couldn't be traced back to them, not a production account with their name plastered all over it. If Alibaba had wanted a model to call home, I'd expect it to have done a far better job.

With that said, this isn't harmless, especially given that the Singapore host is a live deployment. Every time the model decides to fetch one of these URLs, the owner of that bucket can see your IP address, the time, and the full URL. There's also a separate problem: a model that confidently invents its own history, and then invents a correction when asked to check that history, makes its self-reports unreliable as an audit trail. The fix, if you're running Qwen 3.8 as an agent, is to deny outbound network access by default, and block requests to hosts that never appeared anywhere in the conversation before the model tried to fetch them.

Alibaba hasn't said anything publicly about any of this, and it's the only one that can confirm what its training environment looks like. However, everything I've seen seems to support the idea that the model spent a lot of time fetching pages through Alibaba's own proxy, and as a result, it now holds an incredibly strong relationship in its weights between fetching web pages and an internal proxy it used during post-training.

Is it sloppy? Undoubtedly, but the evidence strongly suggests that this is just a model remembering its training environment, rather than one deliberately engineered to send information about its users back home.

item.title: Those US-made laptops BlueChip is building may get Starlink-like antennas, too
item.itunes:title: Those US-made laptops BlueChip is building may get Starlink-like antennas, too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Anduril and Qualcomm launch BlueChip laptops, with 90% of the cost using US and allied parts.
  • BlueChip's replaceable top shell could house flat phased-array antennas for Starlink-like satellite links.
  • Built for government, defense, and first responders; may bring satellite-ready consumer laptops later.

In case you missed it, Anduril and Qualcomm announced earlier today that they were entering a partnership to create a range of laptops using US production lines. The range is called BlueChip, and while it's not wholly produced on US soil for the time being, 90% of the cost comes from American and Allied-made parts, with a goal to raise it to 100% eventually. Now, one of Anduril's co-founders, Palmer Luckey, has hinted that they may also get an antenna that can connect to satellite services like Starlink.

Palmer Luckey hints that BlueChip may get Starlink-like antennas

It's not a guarantee, but it is promising

As spotted by PCMag, Luckey presented a video on the Anduril Industries YouTube account. Titled "BlueChip: Rebuilding American Computer Manufacturing," Luckey details how the BlueChip is made out of metals that America "knows how to extract, knows how to refine, knows how to process, and knows how to mill at scale at a reasonable price." Part of the design is that the laptop should survive harsh conditions, and Luckey explains how the BlueChip achieves that:

"And so what we've designed is a chassis that makes it very, very easy to replace the bottom shell and even the top shell, which you can easily integrate things like, uh, solar panels, other soft goods, other service insignias, even things like flat phased array antennas directly into the laptop itself."

Take note of that last item he listed: flat phased array antennas. They're used to connect to satellite internet networks like Starlink, which means that, down the road, these laptops could potentially support a top-shell attachment that connects straight to orbit. Of course, they may not actually use Starlink specifically, but it's still pretty exciting.

It makes a ton of sense, as Anduril and Qualcomm hope to get these laptops to people working in "government, defense, first responders, and public safety," where losing internet connection is simply not an option. However, if BlueChip ever decides to go into consumer tech, we may get laptops with antennas that connect directly to satellites.

Qualcomm isn't ruling out Snapdragon X2-powered gaming handhelds

There's nothing technically stopping manufactures from releasing gaming handhelds powered by the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Windows 11 has a “feature” that throttles performance, but disabling it has a security tradeoff
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 has a “feature” that throttles performance, but disabling it has a security tradeoff
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's rare that a security vulnerability affects a huge swath of processors all at once, but the Spectre vulnerabilities that were uncovered in 2018 were so widespread that they forced operating system vendors to trade performance for protection. Windows started carrying mitigations to protect against it that were on by default, and it did take sacrificing some CPU performance. They're still enabled by default today, and users can switch it off if they please with a simple registry tweak. Whether doing so is a smart optimization measure or just an unnecessary risk depends on what the machine is used for and the age of the CPU, and the latter matters a lot more than it used to.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
This one Windows 11 update made my PC faster and consume less RAM, and I didn't change a single setting

There's no reason not to upgrade to 26H2

By  Abhinav Raj

The Spectre mitigations are still active

A family of attack vectors on speculative execution

Spectre is a family of different attacks on the same processor technique called speculative execution, which is used in virtually every modern CPU. Processors use this technique to stay fast by guessing ahead as to where the code will go, and discarding the incorrect guesses. Traces of those incorrect guesses linger in the cache, and with a carefully written program, someone could feasibly infer sensitive data based on those traces. The variant that takes advantage of that mechansim is the Spectre variant 2, or branch target injection, where an attacker trains the CPU's branch predictor to steer the speculation somewhere useful for them, such as into the kernel code that handles secrets.

The mitigations that Windows put in place restricts that kind of speculation that happens at the boundary between apps and the kernel, and that's where the performance cost lies. It's not a throttle as much as it is just a bit of extra work that happens every time a program hands something off to the OS. Workloads that cross a lot of boundaries of the system often, like storage and code compiling, feel this a lot more. Anything that runs solely on the CPU cores themselves and doesn't call into the kernel won't really notice a performance impact.

7 apps that could be slowing your Windows performance

Is your Windows laptop feeling sluggish? These seven apps could be affecting performance.

6
By  Saeed Wazir

The performance cost can be real

Microsoft admitted that it can have a significant impact

When Microsoft shipped these mitigations in 2018, it released them along with their own testing, which showed single-digit slowdowns on WIndows 10 PCs with Skylake or newer Intel processors. On Haswell and older, some benchmarks showed larger drops that users would definitely feel a bit more. Microsoft also noted that the first Spectre variant and Meltdown could be patched without significant slowdowns, which left variant 2 as the expensive one to patch as far as performance went.

The registry value FeatureSettingsOverride controls which OS-side mitigations are turned on, and there are some free utilities out there that you can use to turn these off without regedit along with others, such as the mitigations for Meltdown. If you were to change the registry value to the value most commonly shared online, 3, you would disable Meltdown protection as well, while a value of 1 turns off only the Spectre variant 2 mitigation. Either way, the change affects only the operating system’s side of the defense.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

Newer CPUs don't benefit as much

The newer you get, the less you gain from turning off Spectre mitigations

  • Credit: htomari | Flickr
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons
  • Credit: htomari | Flickr
  • Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Newer chips fix some of these flaws directly in silicon and make the rest cheaper to mitigate, and Windows itself moved to lower-overhead mitigation techniques like retpoline back in 2019. On a recent Ryzen or Intel processor, disabling the mitigation in the OS probably won’t give you any measurable performance increase. The risk of doing so also isn't purely theoretical, either. In 2021, researcher Julien Voisin found working Spectre exploits for Windows and Linux uploaded to VirusTotal. They were traced back to Immunity’s commercial penetration-testing platform, Canvas. Later, in 2024, researchers at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam demonstrated an attack called Native BHI that leaked kernel memory on Intel systems running Linux despite the protections already being in place, and Microsoft has continued publishing guidance for newer variants.

Of course, for these types of exploits, malicious code has to exist and be actively running on the machine, so something that exclusively plays games or lives in the living room as a media box isn't really at risk for these types of exploits. Turning off Spectre might not net you a terrible amount of performance, but Microsoft does point to Memory Integrity and the Virtual Machine Platform as features that can hurt performance in specific scenarios, though turning those off comes with their own set of potential security trade-offs.

I make this one change to make Windows faster

One simple toggle can speed up your Windows experience

15
By  Ty Sherback

Spectre mitigations are there for a reason

While disabling Spectre mitigations to increase performance isn't a complete myth, they're not nearly as effective as the used to be. On a decade-old processor, it can return real performance to workloads that lean on the kernel and cross between different components on the system, but on a modern CPU, it trades away protection for a few benchmark points. Whether that's worth it for you will come down to your specific system and workload.

item.title: I explored 5 code editors beyond VS Code, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:title: I explored 5 code editors beyond VS Code, and one was clearly ahead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
VS Code has become my go-to recommendation for coding, but I started wondering what I might be missing by sticking with the same editor. There are plenty of alternatives out there, each with its own approach to writing and managing code. So, I decided to explore five options that caught my attention, from traditional text editors to AI-powered coding environments. I wanted to see what made each one worth considering, where they fell short, and whether any could offer a better everyday experience. One of them surprised me more than I expected.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Kate

A simple text editor that does more than I expected

Kate felt like a practical option when I wanted an editor that stayed out of my way. It comes with a clean interface, syntax highlighting for multiple programming languages, and useful features that make working with code easier. I particularly liked its split-view editing, which let me work with two files side by side without constantly switching between tabs.

Kate also includes a built-in terminal, making it convenient to run commands without leaving the editor. Its session support helps me pick up where I left off, while the search and replace tools make navigating larger files less tedious. However, Kate feels more like a traditional text editor than a modern development environment. It's a solid choice for everyday editing, but I wanted something more ambitious.

Devin Desktop

A different approach to getting coding work done

Devin Desktop caught my attention because it takes a different approach to working with code. Rather than focusing only on editing files, it brings Devin's AI software engineering capabilities into a desktop environment. I could use it to delegate coding tasks, work through project requirements, and let an AI agent handle parts of the implementation.

What interested me most was the idea of moving beyond asking for code suggestions and giving an agent a more complete task to work on. This approach could be useful when I need to explore an unfamiliar codebase or tackle repetitive development work. However, I still needed to review the output carefully and make sure the changes matched my requirements.

Devin Desktop felt more like a workspace for AI-assisted development than a conventional code editor. That distinction made it interesting, although it wasn't quite the traditional editing experience I was looking for.

Cursor

AI features that fit naturally into my coding workflow

The familiar interface made it easy for me to get started without spending much time learning a new layout. What stood out was how easily I could ask questions about my code, generate changes, and work with multiple files using natural-language instructions.

I found its codebase awareness particularly useful. Instead of explaining every file and function manually, I could ask it to help me understand how different parts of a project worked together. Its inline editing also made it convenient to refine existing code without interrupting my workflow.

However, AI is central to the experience, and getting the most out of it means relying on AI throughout development. I liked the convenience, but I wanted to see whether another editor could offer a better overall balance of performance, simplicity, and everyday usability.

I compared VS Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity for 30 days, and one pulled far ahead

One tool simply felt ahead.

15
By  Parth Shah

Nevoim

A keyboard-driven editor that rewards patience

I had to adjust my usual editing habits to get comfortable with Neovim. It uses a keyboard-focused, modal editing system, so I could navigate files, select text, and make changes without constantly reaching for the mouse. Once I started getting used to its commands, even routine editing tasks felt more efficient.

What impressed me was how much control it offered. I could customize the editor with Lua, add plugins for my preferred workflow, and use its built-in language server support for features such as code navigation and diagnostics. Its terminal integration was another useful addition, keeping common development tasks close at hand.

The downside was the learning curve. Neovim requires more setup and patience than most graphical editors. I appreciated its flexibility, but I wanted an editor that felt powerful without demanding so much configuration.

Zed

The editor that got the balance right

What stood out to me about Zed was its focus on performance. Built with Rust, it is designed to keep editing responsive without the overhead of an Electron-based editor. Moving between files, navigating projects, and working with multiple panes felt smooth. I also liked how the clean interface kept the focus on my code instead of surrounding it with too many panels and menus.

Zed offers several useful features without requiring me to build my entire workflow around extensions. Its built-in Git integration lets me review changes, inspect diffs, and manage my work directly in the editor. Language server support adds familiar development features such as code completion, diagnostics, and navigation, while the integrated terminal lets me run commands without switching applications.

I was also interested in its approach to AI and collaboration. Zed supports AI-assisted coding, including inline edits and chat, with options to connect different model providers. Its real-time collaboration features let developers work together in a shared editing environment.

After a month with VS Code, Cursor, and Zed, I finally found the editor that gets out of the way

I spent a month switching editors, and one finally made me stop looking.

3
By  Yash Patel

The editor that earned a place in my workflow

Exploring these five editors reminded me that the most popular tool isn't always the right fit for everyone. Each one has something different to offer, but Zed stood out as the editor I wanted to spend more time with. It balances a focused interface with useful features without making the experience feel complicated. VS Code remains a solid choice, but if you're curious about trying something new, Zed deserves a spot on your shortlist.

Zed

Zed is an open-source, high-performance code editor and modular development environment (IDE) designed for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Kate

A simple text editor that does more than I expected

Kate felt like a practical option when I wanted an editor that stayed out of my way. It comes with a clean interface, syntax highlighting for multiple programming languages, and useful features that make working with code easier. I particularly liked its split-view editing, which let me work with two files side by side without constantly switching between tabs.

Kate also includes a built-in terminal, making it convenient to run commands without leaving the editor. Its session support helps me pick up where I left off, while the search and replace tools make navigating larger files less tedious. However, Kate feels more like a traditional text editor than a modern development environment. It's a solid choice for everyday editing, but I wanted something more ambitious.

Devin Desktop

A different approach to getting coding work done

Devin Desktop caught my attention because it takes a different approach to working with code. Rather than focusing only on editing files, it brings Devin's AI software engineering capabilities into a desktop environment. I could use it to delegate coding tasks, work through project requirements, and let an AI agent handle parts of the implementation.

What interested me most was the idea of moving beyond asking for code suggestions and giving an agent a more complete task to work on. item.title: I thought my car's USB port was just for charging until I discovered what else it could do
item.itunes:title: I thought my car's USB port was just for charging until I discovered what else it could do
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My car's USB port doesn't always get much use. For the most part, I've switched to the 12V socket and a hub for faster charging. So lately, I've been thinking about ways to use that extra port.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Sure, charging is one option, but there have to be more ways to use it. Turns out there is. From playing music stored on a flash drive to connecting an old iPod, it solves a few problems that I hadn't even thought of. Here's everything you need to know.

My car's USB port lets me use my iPod in my car

USB gives me better controls than an auxiliary cable

I'm one of the few who never stopped using iPods for listening to music. Yes, I'm aware that Apple's old-school music player is back in fashion, but for me, it never went away. But when I'm in my car, I want to bring that same music with me. I'd previously connected my iPod to my car with a 3.5mm audio cable, but that meant I didn't have access to any controls, and the audio quality wasn't quite as good as it could be. Surely there has to be a better way.

That's where the car's USB port comes in. On a lark, I plugged my iPod into the car's USB port and switched to the USB input in my car's infotainment system. As it turns out, my car supports connecting to the iPod as a music player.

All I have to do is plug in my iPod, and it can pull up my artists, albums, genres, tracks, and more right there on the infotainment system. This gives me a full-fledged offline music library in my pocket that I can play in my car. That said, keep in mind this won't work with every car. I have an older car that still supports the Made for iPod protocol so that it can communicate with the iPod, but many newer cars no longer support it. Instead, they may recognize the iPod as a hard drive.

I switched back to wired Android Auto and CarPlay, and I don't miss wireless for one key reason

A wired connection is generally more reliable, more so when you are using an external adapter

8
By  Kazim Alvi

USB-powered LED strips can add ambient lighting to an older car

A USB flash drive is a versatile way to add an offline library to your car, too

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

iPods are cool, but they're far from the most convenient way to carry music around in 2026. If you want to carry your offline music library around, a USB flash drive is a solid solution.

All you have to do is copy a selection of albums, playlists, or even audiobooks, plug it into your car's USB port, and select USB media as your input. Even if I'm using Spotify, I keep a USB drive full of favorites plugged into my car's USB port for when I lose internet connectivity. As a fan of live albums and bootlegs, most of which are not available on streaming, this is also how I'm able to listen to my favorite Rush concerts while driving down the expressway. But I digress.

It's a solid backup with the added benefit of impeccable audio quality that streaming services can't match. Of course, a car's USB port isn't only for music playback. The obvious one is wired Android Auto. It gives me a more reliable connection to the car's infotainment system and reduces battery strain. It also prevents my phone from overheating during wireless charging. It's a no-brainer for long drives.

Elsewhere, I'm a fan of ambient lighting in cars, but unfortunately, my car is just a bit too old for it. So, I've experimented with adding USB-powered LED strips around the front of the console. Is it deeply integrated into the car? No, of course not. But does it work? Absolutely. There's no shortage of things to experiment with. Lately, you can even buy USB-powered vacuum cleaners to clean up bits of dirt and debris in your car. That's one experiment that I wasn't too fond of, and I went back to a 12V-powered car vacuum cleaner for the extra power.

Your car's USB port is more useful than it looks

A USB port isn't the most glamorous piece of tech in a car, but it's one of the most versatile. From expanding your media options to enabling features like flash drive-based playback, there's a lot to like. But it gets even better. With low-powered USB tchotchkes like LED light strips or a car vacuum cleaner, you can build a surprisingly versatile in-car setup with almost zero friction.

It takes no extra wiring beyond plugging into a USB cable, adds no extra strain on your car, and is completely reversible when you're done. What's not to like here?

USB-C Universal Cable with Kevlar

Nomad’s 1.5-meter white USB-C cable combines Kevlar reinforcement, a durable nylon weave, and metal connectors for everyday use. It supports charging up to 240W with compatible devices and chargers, while an integrated silicone tie keeps it tidy between uses.

$50 at Nomad
I went back to a plain USB cable for Android Auto, and I don't miss wireless one bit

Wireless is an upgrade until it stops feeling like one
